name: AXOS FINANCIAL

devils_advocate.strongest_counter: The strongest case against my no_edge is that Axos is genuinely cheap once the engine's error is removed. On the corrected three-year ROTCE of 18.2% the justified multiple is 1.75 against an actual 1.82 — but the justified-P/TBV form uses a fixed 2.0% terminal growth for a bank whose tangible book per share is compounding 17.6% a year and whose assets grew 20.9%. At g = 4% the justified multiple is 1.78 and at g = 5% it is 1.96, i.e. the stock is fair to cheap. That is the ENVA bias in this file, and it marks fast-compounding lenders expensive by construction. A grower this fast arguably deserves more than a Gordon model with g pinned at 2%.
devils_advocate.what_would_prove_it: Four more quarters of ROTCE at or above 17% with tangible book per share still compounding above 12%, and a credit performance through the rate move that does not require a step-up in provisioning. Concretely: fiscal 2027 Q1 and Q2 net income above $125M with net charge-offs in the commercial real estate book below 40bp annualised.
devils_advocate.already_visible: Partly. The compounding is visible and verified in the 10-K — tangible book per share $37.26 to $44.60 to $50.96 across three years, which is a 17% CAGR, and the return has been above 16% in each of them. What is NOT visible is any observation of this loan book through a tightening cycle: the Fed is expected to raise on 16 September and Axos grew loans 20%+ into it. Goldman's figure that 32% of Russell 2000 companies carry floating-rate debt is a borrower-side risk that lands on Axos's asset quality, not just on its own funding.
devils_advocate.unresolved: I could not decompose fiscal 2026's $490.4M into spread income versus gains on purchased loan portfolios, so I cannot say what share of the 16.3% return is repeatable underwriting and what share is opportunistic purchasing. That is the difference between a 17% and a 13% sustainable ROTCE, and it is the whole verdict. I also did not obtain the commercial real estate concentration ratio or the criticised-asset trend, which is the load-bearing credit question on a bank that grew loans $4.5 billion in twelve months.

what_changed: Fiscal 2026 10-K filed 2026-08-20 (fiscal year ended 30 June 2026): net income $490.4M vs $432.9M; common stockholders' equity $3,166.4M vs $2,680.7M; tangible book value per common share $50.96 vs $44.60; return on average common stockholders' equity 16.32% / 17.30% / 21.64% for FY2026/25/24. Q4 FY26 net income $124.9M, diluted EPS $2.16, adjusted EPS $2.53. The Verdant acquisition is inside the commercial & industrial loan growth. No company-specific news in the 90-day store — the tape was quiet (5d -2.3%, 0.7x volume) and the name was picked by rotation, not by an event.
consensus_case: Axos is a $30B-asset branchless bank compounding tangible book per share at 17.6% a year ($55.81 book value per share at 30 June 2026 from $47.46) while earning a return on average common equity of 16.3% in fiscal 2026, 17.3% in 2025 and 21.6% in 2024 — the company's own figures from the 10-K. Total assets grew 20.9% to $30.0 billion on $4.5 billion of net loan growth, deposits grew $3.7 billion, and fiscal 2026 net income was $490.4 million against $432.9 million. A buyer at 1.82x tangible book is paying roughly ten times earnings for a bank that has out-earned its cost of equity every year of the cycle, funds itself with low-cost digital deposits, and has repeatedly bought distressed loan books (FDIC portfolios, Verdant) at wide spreads. At a 17-18% sustainable return on tangible common equity and an 11.3% cost of equity, 1.8x tangible book is close to arithmetically correct, not a premium.
base_case_rationale: Not applicable — book method. See rotce_override. My sustainable ROTCE is 17%, below the three-year computed average of 18.2% and below the 20%+ Axos printed in fiscal 2024, because the fiscal 2024 number was flattered by gains on purchased FDIC loan portfolios that are a repeatable strategy but not a repeatable margin, and because a 20% ROTCE on a $30B balance sheet invites the competition that compresses it. 17% is still a return roughly six points above the cost of equity, which is what the multiple has to be built on.
key_risks: The 16-21% return is the input the entire verdict rests on and I could not separate repeatable spread income from opportunistic distressed-loan purchase gains
Loans grew $4.5 billion (20%+) in the twelve months immediately before an expected Fed hike; credit cost on that vintage is unobserved
Commercial real estate concentration not quantified in this pass
The justified-P/TBV model's fixed 2% terminal growth systematically marks a bank compounding tangible book at 17.6% as expensive — the recorded gap is sensitive to a constant, not to the business
Digital-deposit funding advantage narrows if deposit competition re-intensifies at higher policy rates
watch_for: Fiscal 2027 Q1 (September quarter) net income and whether ROTCE holds above 16% with the quarter's loan growth
Net charge-offs and criticised assets in commercial real estate after the September FOMC
Any disclosure separating purchased-loan accretion from core net interest income
Tangible book value per common share growth falling below 10% annualised — that is the signal the compounding thesis has ended
